quarterly_data.signal: RECORD BACKLOG OF $53 BILLION - and the big work is not in it yet. Duke Austin: 'The record backlog we reported reflects the demand in front of us, but we're still in the early stages. The larger programs across the utility generation and technology load center markets are ahead of us, and we expect them to stack in the years to come.' The 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV transmission are still in engineering ('We're not in backlog on any of the bigger work yet'), and about 95% of the generation work is not in backlog either. He expects record backlog again in the third quarter and probably the fourth. Book-to-burn will be lumpy: 1:1 to 1:2 in ordinary quarters, 1:5 to 1:6 in quarters when big chunks of projects land (the 765 kV work brought in last quarter was that kind of boost) - 'lower lows and higher highs all the way through'. A large share of the technology work never touches backlog at all: MEP crews can 'book and bill $300 million on a site in a quarter' against an MSA and 'you never see it show up in backlog'. CFO Jayshree Desai on data-center backlog discipline: only items with limited notices to proceed go in, 'we don't put the rest in until the project is a confirmed go.'

quarterly_data.signal: Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
quarterly_data.figure: 85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

quarterly_data.signal: The stacking has not started. Duke Austin: the 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV projects and the generation work are 'just starting - a lot of it's in engineering'; they start hitting backlog in the later half of this year, crews go to the field around the second half of 2027, and the compounding effect then stacks out 'throughout what I would consider the decade' and 'well past 2030'. He compares it to 2012-2015, when a batch of big projects compounded, and says the base business is doing upper-single-digit to double-digit growth before any of that lands. The nearest concrete catalyst named on the call is the NiSource generation award: 'I do believe a significant amount of that will go into backlog in the third quarter.'

quarterly_data.signal: VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
quarterly_data.figure: HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

quarterly_data.signal: Technology is now 15% to 20% of Quanta's business - 'a spectrum from chips to everything, not just data centers' - grown to that share over the last two years off the Cupertino Electric platform, and Duke Austin frames it as a second TAM 'every bit as big as our utility TAM'. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.
quarterly_data.figure: Technology = 15% to 20% of the business; Quanta can self-perform 80% to 90% of a data-center build

quarterly_data.signal: WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

quarterly_data.signal: Management listed four new and developing uses of battery storage by large energy users such as data centers and C&I facilities. (1) Speed to power: storage speeds grid interconnection by matching power demand to grid capability and avoids the delays and expense of grid upgrades. (2) Quality of power: injecting reactive power to resolve voltage disturbances, managing demand (including disconnecting from the grid when needed) and smooth ramp-rate control. (3) Backup power: replacing higher-cost, carbon-intensive thermal gensets. (4) Support of on-site, bring-your-own generation behind the meter. Quality of power needs a response time below ten milliseconds; Fluence has a road map to deliver it, and this is where it competes with other technologies. Current data-center demand comes more from speed-to-power and bring-your-own-generation applications than from quality of power. Management cited product density, safety, reliability and cybersecurity as advantages, and noted that Fluence does not compete with its data-center customers.

quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED LOAD RISES TO 63 GW through 2030, up from 56 GW last quarter, after AEP 'contracted an additional 7 GW of load coming mostly from AEP Texas and AEP Ohio.' CEO Bill Fehrman: 'Of the 63 GW, nearly 90% are data centers which include hyperscalers, while the rest are industrials.' 53 GW are in Texas and Ohio and need large-scale transmission; the remaining 10 GW requires new generation. By region: PJM contracted load increased by approximately 1 gigawatt (mainly Ohio, substantially all backed by take-or-pay ESAs); SPP increased by approximately 1 GW, driven primarily by an Amazon data center project in Northwest Louisiana (almost half of incremental SPP load now on take-or-pay ESAs); ERCOT accounted for the majority of growth, rising to 41 GW from 36 GW. Customers must meet investment-grade credit, parent guarantees or other credit support. Mihalik: last fall's $72 billion capital plan was set alongside a 28 GW contracted-load outlook, so the jump to 63 GW 'really implies a meaningful upside to our current capital plan.'

The vast majority of demand growth is driven by steady and consistent batches of cloud and inference data center modules, limiting reliance on any single project or customer. Starting in January 2027, large load customers with demand of 25 megawatts or greater face minimum demand charges, and new ESAs carry firm contract terms with exit fees and enhanced collateral. Virginia data center load has grown at a 20% CAGR since 2016 while residential rates averaged 9% below the national average. Other large customers are not being crowded out, and on a Virginia Senate proposal that could remove a data center tax benefit, management said the outcome is hard to predict but it expects data center growth to continue.
quarterly_data.figure: over 48 gigawatts in contracting stages as of December 2025 (around 47 gigawatts as of September; approximately 1.4 gigawatts or 3% increase); 20-plus gigawatts of signed ESA and CLOA contracts; data center load 20% CAGR since 2016

quarterly_data.signal: Five-year total capital estimate raised from $50 billion to approximately $65 billion, a 30% increase; over 90% of the increase is at Dominion Energy Virginia, 'home to the largest data center market in the world'; nearly two-thirds of the updated spend is eligible for rider recovery (subject to regulatory approval); investment base CAGR updated to approximately 10%. Growth spans electric transmission and distribution, with a notable increase in generation. Management continues to see additional investment across the value chain, biased towards the early 2030s and beyond, that is not yet in the plan. There is no capital for an SMR in this five-year plan (nuclear technology evaluation is still in its final stages).
quarterly_data.figure: from $50 billion to approximately $65 billion, representing a 30% increase; over 90% at Dominion Energy Virginia; investment base CAGR approximately 10%

quarterly_data.signal: Gas generation in the capital plan includes two CTs and three CCGTs, and Dominion has secured turbine slots for each project; the CCGT projects have projected in-service dates of 2032 through 2034. On November 25 the Virginia SCC approved the certificate of public convenience and necessity and rider for the Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center, an approximately one-gigawatt gas-fired facility expected to cost approximately $1.5 billion and enter service in 2029 (a petition for reconsideration was denied on February 12). Gas generation converts to cash slowly at first, and the projects deliver full cash flow once they enter service in the early 2030s.
quarterly_data.figure: turbine slots secured for two CTs and three CCGTs; CCGT in-service dates of 2032 through 2034; Chesterfield approximately one-gigawatt, approximately $1.5 billion, in service in 2029

quarterly_data.signal: On February 13 PJM announced its final selections in the latest transmission open window process, awarding Dominion a portfolio of projects totaling over $5 billion with in-service dates through 2032, the largest proposed investment by Dominion Energy Virginia since PJM began its open window process; much of it is in the updated capital plan, and some extends beyond 2030.
quarterly_data.figure: over $5 billion of PJM open window transmission projects; in-service dates through 2032

quarterly_data.signal: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind is over 70% complete and on track to deliver first power to the grid by March: all 176 monopiles were installed faster than expected, the third and final offshore substation is installed, and deepwater export cables are in; around 70% of towers and nacelles and 30% of blades are fabricated; the first turbine was completed in January. The budget is $11.5 billion, including unused contingency of $155 million, and covers weather-delay contingency through July 2027; each additional quarter beyond that would add between $150 million and $200 million, part of it allocated to the financing partner (Stonepeak, under existing contractual provisions). Most turbines are expected in 2026 and some in 2027, at about 2.25 days per installation, and the rider assumes 50% deliverability until PJM network upgrades are done. Management calls CVOW the fastest way to bring significant low-cost electricity to customers 'who are leading the AI race'.
quarterly_data.figure: over 70% complete; budget $11.5 billion including unused contingency of $155 million; between $150 million and $200 million per additional quarter; 2.25 days per installation; 50% deliverability assumed

quarterly_data.signal: Millstone nuclear supplies over 90% of Connecticut's carbon-free electricity. 55% of its output is under a fixed-price contract through late 2029 (the PPA expires in August '29), the remainder is derisked by hedging, and its 2025 capacity factor was over 91%. Connecticut DEEP issued a zero-carbon energy RFP in January (bids due in March, evaluation coordinated with other New England states), with clarity on the outcome expected towards the back half of the year. Dominion is still evaluating support for incremental data center activity at Millstone, which it says must be pursued collaboratively with Connecticut stakeholders.
quarterly_data.figure: 55% of output under fixed-price contract through late 2029; capacity factor of over 91% in 2025

quarterly_data.signal: Financing the five-year plan: nearly 60% of investing cash flows and dividends comes from internal operating cash flow, about 10% from net hybrid issuance, 10% or so from common equity through the DRIP and ATM programs, and roughly 20% from long- and short-term debt. Equity issuance averages roughly 2.5% of market cap annually; about a third of the five-year equity falls in 2026-2028 and about two-thirds in 2029-2030, when the largest capital increases (particularly gas generation spend) occur.

contracts.signal: Georgia Power signed a 3.2 GW, 25-year contract for electric service with OpenAI at OpenAI's recently announced site near Savannah, Georgia. The site is expected to take electric service in phases beginning in 2028 and features 1 GW of flexible demand response to support reliability when system demand is highest - Southern's first flexible-demand arrangement with a data center. The contract carries the standard large-load framework: minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, termination/default payments backed by collateral (lines of credit and surety bonds in this case) targeting an A- or better equivalent position. Womack noted the contract pushes Georgia beyond its recently approved generation capacity by right around 1 GW.
contracts.units: 3.2 GW of contracted load, including 1 GW of flexible demand response; service phased in beginning 2028

quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED AI/DATA-CENTER LOAD CROSSES 17 GW. Four large-load projects were signed in the quarter alone: three projects in Alabama where Alabama Power added approximately 3 GW, plus a Georgia Power 3.2 GW, 25-year electric service contract with OpenAI at its newly announced site near Savannah, Georgia. Combined, those four projects represent 6 GW of newly contracted customer load, and together with agreements previously signed they bring total contracted large load agreements across Southern's electric subsidiaries to over 17 GW by the mid-2030s. CEO Christopher Womack framed the vertically integrated, state-regulated model (one-stop shop across generation, transmission and distribution) as the differentiator winning hyperscaler and data-center developer business in the Southeast.
quarterly_data.figure: 6 GW newly contracted in Q2 (Alabama ~3 GW + Georgia Power/OpenAI 3.2 GW); total contracted large load over 17 GW by mid-2030s

quarterly_data.signal: PROSPECTIVE LARGE-LOAD PIPELINE STILL ABOVE 75 GW, WITH 8 GW IN LATE-STAGE NEGOTIATION. Womack: new projects continue to be added to the prospective pipeline of large industrial and data-center projects, 'which remains well above 75 GW.' Beyond the 17 GW already contracted there are an additional 8 GW of projects in late stages, including 3 GW projected to be finalized in the near term; CFO David Poroch said those contracts are likely to go into 2028 and beyond, with a couple of them initiating their ramp-up in 2028 and running into the next decade. Womack also noted momentum migrating west, with 100 MW projects already succeeding in Mississippi and increasing activity there and in Alabama.
quarterly_data.figure: Prospective pipeline well above 75 GW; 8 GW late-stage of which 3 GW near-term; 100 MW projects in Mississippi

quarterly_data.signal: DATA-CENTER LOAD ACTUALLY ON THE SYSTEM IS COMPOUNDING FAST. System-wide data-center load now exceeds 1.2 GW, an increase of more than 500 megawatts over the prior year, and Poroch noted the company 'crossed over the 1,000 MW line this particular quarter.' Data-center usage was 55% higher than Q2 2025 and is up 49% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from large-load customers. That pulled weather-normal commercial sales up 7.4% in Q2 (+6% year to date) and total weather-normal retail electricity sales up 2.3% in the first half - the highest retail sales growth through June in nearly two decades. Q2 adjusted EPS was $1.13, up $0.21 versus Q2 2025 and $0.13 above the company's own estimate; first-half adjusted EPS was $2.46.
quarterly_data.figure: Data-center load >1.2 GW (+500 MW YoY); data-center usage +55% YoY in Q2, +49% YTD; commercial sales +7.4% Q2; Q2 adjusted EPS $1.13

quarterly_data.signal: GUIDANCE RAISED TO THE TOP OF THE RANGE ON LOAD GROWTH. Management now projects full-year 2026 adjusted earnings to be near or at the top of the $4.50-$4.60 adjusted EPS guidance range, with a Q3 adjusted EPS estimate of $1.50 per share, and reiterated the goal of being toward the top half of the long-term earnings trajectory. Drivers named were increased usage and customer growth, higher AFUDC from ongoing construction projects, higher earnings from equity-method investments, and contributions from Southern Company Gas and PowerSecure, where distributed, backup and bridge power solutions markets for data centers continue to expand.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance $4.50-$4.60, now expected near or at the top; Q3 estimate $1.50

quarterly_data.signal: GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.
quarterly_data.figure: 10 GW of new company-owned generation approved (thermal/battery/solar) + hundreds of miles of transmission; Georgia capacity ~1 GW oversubscribed after the OpenAI contract

quarterly_data.signal: OPEN RFPs AT ALABAMA POWER AND GEORGIA POWER ARE INCREMENTAL CAPITAL NOT YET IN THE PLAN. Ongoing RFPs at both utilities are procuring additional generation for the early 2030s. Poroch was explicit that 'there is not placeholders in our capital plan... the RFPs that are open in Alabama, the RFPs that are open in Georgia, none of that is contemplated in our capital forecast at the moment,' and gave a sizing rule of thumb of 'about $2 billion or so, a little bit above maybe related to 1 GW of new generating capacity.' Timeline: selections known by year end 2026, a certification process running through much of 2027 with clarity in the latter part of 2027, spend feathering in around 2028, and the generation coming online in the 2030-2031 timeline. Alabama runs a near-parallel schedule.
quarterly_data.figure: Capital rule of thumb ~$2B per 1 GW of new generating capacity; RFP selections by year-end 2026, certification through 2027, generation online 2030-2031

quarterly_data.signal: HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.
quarterly_data.figure: About $21 billion of collateral in aggregate at full ramp across the 17 GW contracted portfolio; minimum bills cover 100% of incremental cost to serve

quarterly_data.signal: FIRST FLEXIBLE-DEMAND DATA CENTER: 1 GW OF DEMAND RESPONSE AT THE OPENAI SITE. The Savannah site features 1 GW of flexible demand response, and Womack confirmed this is the first time Southern has done that for a data center. Poroch said demand-response flexibility 'does enter into all those conversations' and is possible because the three electric jurisdictions are not limited to a tariff and can negotiate bilateral contracts that price hyperscaler flexibility. Womack said technical requirements - how a hyperscaler's operations affect the system and the grid, and whether it can be more than 'just a taker' - are raised very early in every hyperscaler conversation, and that peak shaving from this resource benefits the whole system.
quarterly_data.figure: 1 GW of flexible demand response at the OpenAI Savannah site - Southern's first for a data center

quarterly_data.signal: NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: SOUTHERN POWER TOLLING AGREEMENTS ROLLING OFF ARE BEING RE-AIMED AT HYPERSCALERS. As existing tolling agreements expire, Womack said the team is in the midst of recontracting conversations with a host of counterparties, screened for creditworthiness, and sees upside in pricing versus where the contracts were originally struck - contributing to the durability and length of the long-term plan. Poroch added that conversations with both current and new Southern Power counterparties are 'proving to be very fruitful', covering repricing of expiring contracts into the next decade plus the previously announced uprate/brownfield opportunities, with an update expected later in the year; the business will not 'build something and see who shows up.'
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT ANNOUNCEMENTS IN THE TERRITORY RAN AT THE SECOND-HIGHEST LEVEL EVER. In the last quarter alone, announcements were made for nearly $14 billion of investment and more than 3,000 new jobs across Southern's electric territories, led by several new data-center facilities in Alabama and a new Amazon warehouse in Georgia - the second-highest investment level ever recorded in the electric territories. Womack said there are no state-level moratoriums on data centers in the territory (though some counties have them) and that hyperscalers need to do a better job explaining the benefits, pointing to the OpenAI announcement as the template for community and rate-stability messaging.
quarterly_data.figure: Nearly $14 billion of announced investment and more than 3,000 new jobs in the quarter, led by new data-center facilities in Alabama

quarterly_data.signal: FIRST-QUARTER RESULTS BEAT, DRIVEN BY DATA-CENTER USAGE. CFO David Poroch: first quarter 2026 adjusted EPS was $1.32 per share, $0.09 higher than the first quarter of 2025 and $0.12 above the company's estimate. Primary drivers were meaningful customer growth and increased usage, including from data centers at the state-regulated electric utilities, plus higher gas-utility revenues and higher energy-related revenues at Southern Power, partly offset by higher financing costs and milder weather. Adjusted EPS estimate for the second quarter is $1.00 per share.
quarterly_data.figure: Adjusted EPS $1.32 ($0.09 higher YoY, $0.12 above estimate); second-quarter adjusted EPS estimate $1.00

quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED LARGE LOAD PASSES 11 GW. CEO Chris Womack: in just the last two months the company signed contracts for another 1.9 GW of customer load with high credit quality hyperscalers (Poroch: Georgia Power signed two projects representing 1.9 GW), bringing fully contracted large-load agreements to more than 11 GW across Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi. Demand across the electric territories has culminated in 23 GW of contracted or late-stage load. The bilaterally negotiated agreements are structured so that customers driving incremental demand cover the full share of the cost to serve them.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.9 GW newly contracted with hyperscalers in two months; over 11 GW contracted large load; 23 GW contracted or late-stage

quarterly_data.signal: LATE-STAGE PIPELINE GROWS TO 12 GW; PROSPECTIVE PIPELINE WELL OVER 75 GW. Poroch: interest from large load customers (data centers and large manufacturers) remains strong with a prospective pipeline of well over 75 GW. The company is in active late-stage discussions for another 12 GW of contracted load through the mid-2030s, an increase of 2 GW from last quarter, and roughly 6 GW or half of those late-stage gigawatts are expected to be finalized with executed contracts in the near term. In a little over two months, projects representing 12 GW advanced to the next stage. Womack said activity is migrating west, with greater activity in Alabama and Mississippi while Georgia remains very strong, and noted 'repeat buyers' coming back for more capacity; Poroch said Georgia's collateral requirement is shaking out speculative projects.
quarterly_data.figure: Prospective pipeline well over 75 GW; late-stage 12 GW (+2 GW vs last quarter); roughly 6 GW expected to be contracted near term

quarterly_data.signal: DATA-CENTER USAGE UP 42% YEAR OVER YEAR. Poroch: first-quarter weather-normal retail electricity sales to all classes were 2.3% higher than the first quarter of 2025, the highest first-quarter total retail sales growth in recent history. The commercial class grew 4.5% weather-adjusted, bolstered by data centers; data center usage was up 42% year-over-year, primarily due to accelerating usage ramps at large load facilities. Industrial sales grew 1.5% and 46,000 new residential customers were added.
quarterly_data.figure: Weather-normal retail sales +2.3%; commercial +4.5%; data center usage +42% YoY; industrial +1.5%; 46,000 new residential customers

quarterly_data.signal: GENERATION BUILD FOR LOAD GROWTH: FIRST 10 GW ASSETS ONLINE AND NEW 2-6 GW GEORGIA RFP. Womack: Georgia Power achieved commercial operation of two battery energy storage systems providing nearly 200 MW, the first of the 10 GW portfolio of approved new generation (including battery systems and natural gas combustion turbines projected online later in 2026 and 2027). Poroch: Georgia Power initiated the regulatory process for an all-source RFP to procure 2-6 GW of new dispatchable generation for in-service in 2032 and 2033; company-owned resources selected in the Alabama Power and Georgia Power RFPs would be substantial incremental investment above the base capital plan. Timeline: selection through the rest of this year, certification pretty much through 2027, spend likely initiating in 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: Two battery systems, nearly 200 MW online; 10 GW approved generation portfolio; Georgia all-source RFP for 2-6 GW in service 2032 and 2033

quarterly_data.signal: SOUTHERN POWER GAS-TURBINE UPRATES. Poroch: Southern Power is moving forward with 400 MW of additional capacity through natural gas turbine upgrades at multiple existing facilities in Alabama and Georgia, with commercial operation projected between 2029 and 2031, adding approximately $700 million to the capital plan; an additional 300 MW of natural gas uprates is under evaluation (covering the whole fleet; timing probably over the course of the next year or so). Contracting for the 400 MW is in fairly late-stage conversations; Womack said Southern Power has said numbers 'up in the mid-90s in terms of what's contracted' and that recontracting talks and conversations with potential hyperscalers are both underway. 'we don't take merchant risk.'
quarterly_data.figure: 400 MW uprates, commercial operation between 2029 and 2031, approximately $700 million capex; additional 300 MW under evaluation

quarterly_data.signal: FINANCING THE BUILDOUT: DOE LOANS AND REMAINING EQUITY NEED. Womack highlighted $26.5 billion in loan agreements with the Department of Energy benefiting Alabama and Georgia customers, projected to generate cumulative customer savings of $7 billion over the approximately 30-year term. Poroch: an incremental $500 million of equity was sourced through the ATM program; including the $700 million of Southern Power capex, the remaining need for equity or equity equivalents is approximately $1.8 billion through 2030, on a path to 17% FFO to debt by 2029; incremental capital is expected to be funded about 40% with equity.
quarterly_data.figure: $26.5 billion DOE loans ($7 billion projected customer savings); $500 million ATM equity; remaining equity need approximately $1.8 billion through 2030

quarterly_data.signal: SUPPLY CHAIN FOR THE BUILDOUT - TURBINES, TRANSFORMERS, CABLE AND LABOR. Asked about tight areas, Womack said 'it's not anything you can take for granted' but the headline is the company is 'very well positioned' thanks to its scale and long supplier relationships, and must keep working it 'whether it's turbines, whether it's transformers, whether it's hot wire, cable, name it.' The company has the turbines identified to support its RFPs and holds positions with turbine suppliers and OEMs on both delivery and pricing. He expects some tightness in the labor market and cited some 10,000 laborers at peak on the Vogtle construction as the basis of its labor relationships.

quarterly_data.signal: FY2025 RESULTS: ADJUSTED EPS AT THE TOP OF GUIDANCE, DATA-CENTER USAGE UP 17% FOR A SECOND YEAR. CFO David Poroch: adjusted earnings per share of $4.30 for 2025 was the very top of the 2025 guidance range and represents 6% growth (9% average annual growth from 2023). Weather-normalized total retail electricity sales rose 1.7% versus 2024, 'more than double the cumulative growth we saw over the last decade', with Georgia Power growing 2.5%. Commercial sales were 'led by increased usage from existing and new large load data center customers, which were up 17% year-over-year for the second year in a row'; industrial sales grew 1.4% and the company added 39,000 new residential electric customers. CEO Chris Womack: more than 120 companies located or expanded facilities in the electric and gas territories over the past year, supporting over 21,000 new jobs, and hyperscalers 'have made significant investments in our service territories.'

quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED LARGE LOAD REACHES 10 GW ACROSS 26 PROJECTS; PIPELINE OVER 75 GW. Poroch: robust interest from large load customers, including hyperscalers, has materialized into 26 signed contracts representing 10 gigawatts of fully contracted electric service agreements, 2 gigawatts higher than last quarter and 4 gigawatts higher than a year ago. Nearly all of the 26 projects are under construction, with load ramps totaling 8 gigawatts by the end of the 5-year planning horizon and ultimately 10 gigawatts beyond 2030. The company is in late-stage discussions for another 10 gigawatts, 3 gigawatts of which are 'working through final reviews and are highly likely to progress to an executed contract in the near term'; Poroch confirmed the 2030 plan includes the 10 gigawatts signed plus these 3 gigawatts and nothing beyond. The total large load pipeline has increased to over 75 gigawatts as momentum grows in Alabama and Mississippi. On movement in the Georgia Power large load update, Poroch called it 'normal churn coming in and out of the pipeline' and said the short end of the pipeline 'has contracted a little bit' as counterparties, who also post collateral, refine their needs.
quarterly_data.figure: 26 signed contracts representing 10 gigawatts (2 gigawatts higher than what we reported last quarter and 4 gigawatts higher than a year ago); load ramps totaling 8 gigawatts by the end of the 5-year planning horizon; late-stage discussions for another 10 gigawatts, 3 gigawatts in final reviews; large load pipeline over 75 gigawatts

quarterly_data.signal: LONG-TERM SALES FORECAST RAISED TO 10% A YEAR ON LARGE-LOAD RAMPS. Poroch: retail electric sales across the three electric operating companies are projected to grow at least 3% in 2026, and annual electricity sales growth is projected to average 10% from 2026 through 2030, an increase of 2 percentage points from the prior long-term projection; Georgia Power's total retail electric sales growth is projected at approximately 13% over the same period. Based on the timing of load ramps in the risk-adjusted forecast, sales growth and the associated revenues are projected to accelerate into 2027 'with an even more pronounced expansion in 2028.' Commercial sales, roughly 1/3 of total retail sales, are projected to more than double, growing roughly 20% annually through the end of the decade.
quarterly_data.figure: retail electric sales growth of at least 3% in 2026; annual electricity sales growth of 10% on average from 2026 through 2030 (up 2 percentage points); Georgia Power approximately 13%; commercial sales growing roughly 20% annually

quarterly_data.signal: MULTI-YEAR EPS GUIDANCE INTRODUCED ON LARGE-LOAD GROWTH. Poroch: 2026 adjusted EPS guidance is $4.50 to $4.60 per share (7% growth from the 2025 guidance range), with a first-quarter adjusted EPS estimate of $1.20. The company expects to grow adjusted EPS 8% to 9% from 2026 through 2028 and set initial ranges of $4.85 to $4.95 for 2027 (approximately 8% growth) and $5.25 and $5.45 for 2028 (approximately 9% growth), with approximately 7% to 8% growth longer term from the 2028 range - an average of 8% from the 2026 guidance midpoint to 2030. The outlook is 'supported by a large and growing portfolio of large load contracts'; Poroch said management would be 'pretty disappointed if we didn't achieve near the top end' and sees upside from repricing Southern Power capacity.

quarterly_data.signal: CAPITAL PLAN RAISED TO $81 BILLION, DRIVEN BY NEW GENERATION FOR LARGE LOAD. Poroch: the base capital investment forecast is $81 billion over the next 5 years, 95% of it at the state-regulated utilities, an $18 billion or approximately 30% increase from a year ago, driven mainly by new generation facilities (most announced or approved in 2025) and the approved Georgia IRP (uprates at existing natural gas and nuclear facilities, hydroelectric dam modernization). Roughly $42 billion through 2030 goes to serving projected growth through new generation, enhancements to existing generation and expansions of transmission and interstate pipeline systems, supporting state-regulated rate base growth of approximately 9%. The plan carries no capital placeholders; Alabama Power and Georgia Power RFPs for generation needed in the early to mid-2030s 'could represent several gigawatts of additional new generation', and Poroch gave a rough rule of thumb of $2 billion for a gig of incremental generation. Poroch noted Georgia Power 'just closed in December on 10 gigawatts' and said incremental capital above the plan would be financed with approximately 40% equity or equity equivalents.

quarterly_data.signal: LARGE-LOAD CONTRACT TERMS: 15-YEAR MINIMUMS, TAKE-OR-PAY-STYLE MINIMUM BILLS, COLLATERAL. Poroch: all three electric jurisdictions allow bilaterally negotiated large-load contracts rather than a standard tariff. Data-center contracts carry minimum terms of at least 15 years, fixed or minimum bill provisions 'similar to take-or-pay structures' designed to cover at least 100% of the annual incremental cost to serve (generation and transmission investment, incremental O&M and cost of capital), and termination payments backed by significant collateral requirements. As part of its December certification process for new generation, Georgia Power quantified at least approximately $1.7 billion of benefits lowering the cost to serve existing customers from 2029 through 2031, 'directly attributable to the value created by our approach to contracting'. Load taken beyond the minimum is priced at roughly the marginal cost and is upside to the plan.
quarterly_data.figure: minimum terms of at least 15 years; minimum bills to cover at least 100% of the annual incremental cost to serve; at least approximately $1.7 billion of benefits from 2029 through 2031

quarterly_data.signal: SOUTHERN POWER: GAS FLEET REPRICING AND UPRATES AS UPSIDE OUTSIDE THE PLAN. Womack: Southern Power has over 13 gigawatts of capacity across 55 generating facilities in 15 states, including over 7 gigawatts of natural gas generation in the Southeast, substantially all under long-term contracts. As gas-fleet contracts come up for renewal from the early 2030s, 'The market demand for capacity has increased pricing roughly 2 to 3x higher than where many of these assets are currently contracted', and by 2030 approximately 1,000 megawatts can be remarketed; Poroch cited market examples of 'around $20, maybe $25 a kilowatt month.' The company is in late-stage discussions on uprates of up to an additional 700 megawatts (as soon as '29 per Womack, not included in the plan) and is evaluating 6 brownfield sites in the Southeast for potential new gas development, always under long-term contracts with creditworthy counterparties. Asked whether the uprate capacity would be contracted with co-ops and other power companies rather than sold directly to data centers, Poroch said 'that's a very safe bet.'

quarterly_data.signal: A RARE DOWNWARD REVISION TO A DATA-CENTER PIPELINE — AND WHY IT MATTERS: Exelon's data-center growth pipeline now shows a combined 36 GIGAWATTS, DOWN ROUGHLY 11 GW FROM THE 43 GW previously cited. CFO Jeanne Jones attributes the cut not to demand weakness but to Exelon's own screening discipline: it developed TRANSMISSION SECURITY AGREEMENTS (TSAs) that 'never existed in our regions', and its cluster process now requires a customer to sign a TSA and, importantly, 'PUT UP COLLATERAL BEHIND THAT'. The result: 'what this update reflects is we have now WEEDED OUT SPECULATIVE PROJECTS, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real.' Exelon says it has deliberately kept capex increases consistent with historical levels and only committed capital that was 'certain and durable', alongside its stance on CO-LOCATION and fair cost allocation to shield existing customers from infrastructure costs. This is a useful reality-check datapoint on how much of the headline AI interconnection queue is firm versus speculative.

quarterly_data.signal: PJM supply stress and utility-generation push: during Winter Storm FERN, the PJM RTO had five straight days of peak load between 135 and 140 gigawatts, 97% of the all-time winter peak. Fewer than 1% of Exelon customers lost power. The CEO said the supply challenge is real, and he wants an all-of-the-above answer that includes utility-generated, demand-side and merchant solutions. He cited a Charles River Associates study (management said Exelon enlisted CRA's support): utility-generated power could have saved PJM customers $9.6 to $20 billion in the 2028–2029 delivery year and cut the risk of outages from energy shortages by approximately 85%. Exelon supports PJM's reliability backstop option, backs extending the PJM capacity auction collar, and joined Governor Shapiro's FERC filing. On data-center colocation, Exelon's Colette Honorable (named by the CEO on the call) said "Colocation can be a great solution" and that Exelon took its colocation stance to protect affordability. The CFO said new generation must be built at the right price.
